article.overview: A soil permeability analyser is a class of in-situ instrument intended to measure how readily gas or fluid moves through lunar regolith. Permeability controls gas transport through the soil, which matters for volatile release and retention, and for interpreting how much volatile material a soil may originally have held. The sources reviewed for this article describe a 1971 NASA-contracted permeability probe concept, a gas-permeability test built into the Lunar Volatiles Scout prototype, and laboratory measurements on dry terrestrial and simulant analogues. No flown, dedicated soil permeability analyser was identified.
article.description: The name describes a function rather than a single standard design. A permeability analyser would drive or allow a controlled flow of gas (or, in the earlier concept, a fluid) through a volume of regolith, and convert the resulting pressure or flow behaviour into a permeability value. Permeability is a property of the porous network: it depends on grain size distribution, packing density and the connectivity of pore spaces. Two measurement approaches appear in the sources reviewed. In a steady or equilibrium flow method, a known gas flow is passed through a sample and the resulting pressure difference is measured. In a pressure-decay method, a sealed volume is pressurised with a reference gas and the pressure drop over time is used to derive permeability. The Lunar Volatiles Scout uses the second approach; the laboratory work described in the EGU 2020 abstract uses the first. Neither approach is documented as having operated on the Moon.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purposes described in the sources are to characterise the gas transport properties of lunar regolith in situ, and to use those properties to support volatile inventory estimates. In the Lunar Volatiles Scout design, a permeability test is used to determine how much gas escapes downward through the soil during a volatile extraction sequence, so that the total released gas can be corrected and the original volatile abundance inferred. Permeability data would also be relevant to in-situ resource utilisation planning, because gas transport controls how easily volatiles can be extracted, and to general models of regolith mechanics and gas flow. Applications beyond these are not documented in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: The sources reviewed describe two broad principles. In the pressure-decay approach used by the Lunar Volatiles Scout, the sampler shell is pressurised with a reference gas to a set pressure, and two pressure sensors on either side of an orifice track the pressure. The rate of pressure loss over time gives the soil's gas permeability, from which the abundance of volatiles originally held in the soil can be inferred. In the laboratory method reported by Schweighart et al. (2020), a cylindrical sample is placed in a vacuum chamber between two gas volumes monitored by four pressure sensors. Gas is forced downward through the sample at controlled flow rates, and permeability is calculated from the pressure difference under equilibrium flow. The downward flow direction is chosen to avoid fluidisation of the sample. The 1971 NASA-contracted study describes a permeability probe for measuring fluid flow through porous lunar surface materials, but the NASA record reviewed does not give its measurement method in detail.
article.scientific_importance: Permeability links the physical structure of regolith (grain size, packing density) to how gases move through it. The Lunar Volatiles Scout design uses a pressure-decay test to estimate soil gas permeability and then to infer the original volatile abundance, so permeability is a means to a volatile-inventory estimate rather than an end in itself. Laboratory work on dry analogue materials reports a measured permeability range of 10^-13 to 10^-8 m^2 and finds that grain size distribution and packing density strongly control permeability (Schweighart et al., 2020). Because lunar regolith in situ may differ from laboratory analogues, in-situ measurements are needed to test these relationships under lunar conditions. The sources reviewed do not report any in-situ lunar permeability measurement.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a soil permeability analyser. The sources reviewed describe one prototype with stated design figures, one 1971 experiment definition without published hardware values, and one laboratory apparatus. Values below are tied to these named examples and must not be generalised.

examples.name: Lunar Volatiles Scout (LVS): Volatiles Sampler (VS) with Volatiles Analyser (VA)
examples.type: Prototype; proposed for future missions (not flown)
examples.developers: Technical University of Munich (VS); The Open University (VA); OHB System AG is listed as an author affiliation in the EPSC 2020 abstract.
examples.permeability_function: Pressure-decay test: the sampler shell is pressurised with a reference gas and the pressure drop over time is used to derive soil gas permeability, which is then used to infer the original volatile abundance. Two pressure sensors measure pressure on each side of an orifice.
examples.mass_kg: Stated design figures: VA less than 0.5 kg; VS plus VA less than 1.5 kg (TUM page, no test configuration stated). The EPSC 2020 abstract gives a combined target of less than 2 kg (basis not stated). These figures differ and are not reconciled in the sources.
examples.dimensions_cm: The sampler is described as a 15 cm core drill, but the EPSC 2020 abstract does not say whether 15 cm refers to length, depth or diameter. No other dimensions are published in the sources reviewed.
examples.power: Not stated in the sources reviewed. The sampler uses a heater to release bound volatiles, but no heater power, temperature setpoint or power budget is given.
examples.prospecting_depth_cm: 10 to 20 (mission target stated in the EPSC 2020 abstract)
examples.laboratory_performance: Measured in the laboratory facility, not by the flight heater: sample temperatures from room temperature down to -140 C, and vacuum down to 2e-5 mbar.
examples.technology_readiness: TRL 5 to 6, the authors' own assessment (EPSC 2020 abstract).
examples.qualification: Thermal-vacuum chamber testing of the VS and VA prototype is reported on the TUM page, and the TUM page describes the instrument as in a prototype and ground-test stage. No flight qualification is claimed.

examples.name: Permeability probe concept (Lunar Surface Engineering Properties Experiment definition, Volume 4)
examples.type: Historical experiment definition and probe concept (1971 contractor report)
examples.developers: University of California, Berkeley; NASA contract NAS8-21432
examples.measurement_principle: Measurement of fluid flow through porous lunar surface materials, as stated in the report title and the NASA record header. The method is not described in the NASA record reviewed; the scanned report PDF was not readable in this run.
examples.mass_kg: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.dimensions_cm: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.power: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.flight_status: No evidence of flight was identified. The NASA record does not state whether a probe was built, tested or deployed, and reports no measured results.

examples.name: Laboratory gas-permeability apparatus for dry analogue materials (Schweighart et al., 2020)
examples.type: Laboratory measurement set-up (not a space instrument)
examples.developers: CoPhyLab team (abstract authors: Schweighart, Kargl, Tiefenbacher)
examples.sample_container: Cylindrical container, 4 cm diameter, filled to a sample height of 30 mm.
examples.method: Equilibrium pressure-difference method in a vacuum chamber, with four pressure sensors, a pump in the lower volume, compressed air entering the upper volume, downward gas flow to avoid fluidisation, and flow rates controlled from 0.15 to 19.2 mg/s. Samples were packed on a shaking table.
examples.measured_permeability_range_m2: 10^-13 to 10^-8 across all dry analogue materials tested (glass beads, quartz sand, lunar and Mars simulants, and an asteroid analogue). The abstract gives no value specific to the lunar simulant JSC-1.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions are published for a soil permeability analyser as a whole. The only prototype dimension in the sources reviewed is the 15 cm sampler described in the EPSC 2020 abstract, whose reference dimension is unclear. The 1971 probe and the laboratory apparatus have no dimensions beyond the 4 cm by 30 mm laboratory sample container. A future instrument's dimensions would need to be set by its insertion method, sealed gas volume, orifice geometry and mounting interfaces.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Stated design masses for the Lunar Volatiles Scout are less than 0.5 kg for the VA and less than 1.5 kg for the VS and VA together (TUM page), with a differing combined target of less than 2 kg in the EPSC 2020 abstract. No mass is published for the 1971 probe. Mass matters for launch and lander capacity and must be compared against verified interface limits before any compatibility claim is made.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not stated in the sources reviewed for any example. The Lunar Volatiles Scout sampler is heated to release volatiles, so its power budget would include heater power as well as electronics; no value is published.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A permeability analyser must operate in lunar vacuum and across large surface temperature swings. The TUM page cites a surface temperature swing of about plus or minus 140 K as context for the polar environment. The measurement also depends on the regolith's packing state: insertion or disturbance can change grain packing and therefore permeability, and the sources reviewed do not quantify this effect. A pressure-decay test further requires a stored reference gas, stable pressure sensors with known calibration, and a sealed sample volume. Because the Lunar Volatiles Scout design heats the sample to release volatiles, a permeability test made before and after heating would need to account for any change in the sample state. This is an engineering inference; the sources reviewed do not describe such a sequence. The LVS is designed to insert its sampler to a depth of roughly 10 to 20 cm, which sets the depth of soil characterised.
article.limitations: A dedicated, flown soil permeability analyser has not been identified. The Lunar Volatiles Scout measures permeability as one step of a volatile-extraction sequence rather than as a standalone measurement, and the inferred volatile abundance depends on the gas-transport model used. The laboratory permeability range was measured on dry analogue materials, not on lunar regolith, and spans five orders of magnitude without a simulant-specific value. The 1971 probe is recorded only as an experiment definition with no published measured results.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A soil permeability analyser would most plausibly be a surface instrument, either as a dedicated experiment or as part of a sampling and analysis payload on a rover or lander. No dedicated soil permeability analyser has a verified transport or deployment configuration in the sources reviewed. The Lunar Volatiles Scout is the most developed candidate, and its documented deployment context is the LUVMI rover platform.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument on Earth into a lander or rover payload compartment, with mechanical, thermal, power and data interfaces defined for that vehicle.
Launch the vehicle and transfer it to the Moon.
Land the payload with a lander, or deliver the instrument to the site by rover traverse.

Deploy the sampler: the Lunar Volatiles Scout is designed to be carried by the LUVMI-X rover; the EPSC 2020 abstract gives a rover traverse range of up to 5 km from the lander and a slope capability of up to 20 degrees as targets for the rover, not properties of the instrument.
Insert the sampler into regolith to the target prospecting depth of 10 to 20 cm, which is a mission target.
Provide the reference gas supply, pressure sensors, power and data needed for the pressure-decay test; the supply mechanism is not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Lunar Volatiles Scout is described as a drill-like instrument that is inserted into the regolith from a rover. The EPSC 2020 abstract says the sampler is a 15 cm core drill; the TUM page describes insertion, heating and gas routing to the analyser. The 1971 probe's deployment method is not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No dedicated permeability analyser is documented as having flown. The 1971 probe is an experiment definition study. The Lunar Volatiles Scout is a prototype in ground testing, and the TUM page lists a proposed Phase A study for integration on ispace's Polar Ice Explorer; this is a proposal, not a verified mission.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander or rover is not verified. The proposed ispace Polar Ice Explorer integration is a Phase A proposal and does not establish compatibility. A future permeability analyser would need its mass, dimensions, insertion loads, power, thermal and gas-handling interfaces compared with verified lander or rover specifications before any compatibility claim is made.

article.historical_significance: The 1971 NASA-contracted permeability probe study is an early documented concept for measuring fluid flow in lunar surface materials in situ, produced as an experiment definition under contract NAS8-21432. The Lunar Volatiles Scout, developed by TUM and The Open University with OHB, is a more recent prototype that uses permeability testing as part of a south-pole volatile-prospecting concept. Its laboratory and thermal-vacuum work reached TRL 5 to 6 according to its authors. The primary Lunar Volatiles Scout paper (Biswas et al., 2020) was identified but its full text was not reviewed in this run.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flown or routinely operated instrument named 'soil permeability analyser' was identified. The closest flight-relevant design, the Lunar Volatiles Scout, is a prototype at TRL 5 to 6 whose permeability function is a sub-test of a volatile sampler; its permeability values, sensor specifications and calibration data are not given in the sources reviewed. The 1971 permeability probe is an experiment definition; the NASA record reports no measured results and does not say whether it was built or deployed. Laboratory permeability values come from dry analogues rather than lunar regolith. The Lunar Volatiles Scout mass figures differ between sources, and neither source states the configuration tested. This article's generic engineering discussion describes considerations for a future instrument and is not a certified design specification.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Other images on the TUM Lunar Volatiles Scout page (sampler renders, heater and insertion test photographs) were not included because their processed-derivative asset URLs could not be verified as direct asset links.

data_quality_notes: No flown, dedicated soil permeability analyser was identified in the sources reviewed. The article covers the payload class using a prototype (Lunar Volatiles Scout), a 1971 experiment definition and laboratory apparatus.
An early search summary described the permeability probe as a 1960s NASA work. The NASA record reviewed (NTRS 19720006172) is dated July 1971, so the 1971 date is used.
The NASA 1971 report PDF is a scanned document that could not be read in this run. Its method, dimensions and results are therefore not stated; the NASA record was used for bibliographic data only.

Lunar Volatiles Scout mass figures differ: VA under 0.5 kg and VS plus VA under 1.5 kg (TUM page) versus combined under 2 kg (EPSC 2020 target, basis not stated). Neither is confirmed against a configuration.
The Open University repository (oro.open.ac.uk) and core.ac.uk full texts returned HTTP 403, and the Frontiers article returned HTTP 500; the Biswas et al. 2020 full text was not reviewed.
A search snippet reported an LHS-1 simulant water-permeability value (1.6 x 10^-13 m^2) from a 2023 Acta Astronautica paper; this was not verified against the source and is not used in the article.
The TUM page has no publication date, so the status described (ground-test prototype, Phase A proposals) may be out of date.
